Our reasoning was based on the seasonality and guidance for elevated Treasury issuance and above -target TGA balances, particular ly for the months of July/August and October/November (see US rates: How do you like them ample reserves , dated 18 May). Most of the market started to position this way early on. The Treasury has issued $300bn in bills for July and TGA balances are back to target levels, but repo has still traded at somewhat soft levels – at or slightly below IORB. Most of the tailwinds from repo ha ve come from TGA volatility (particularly on month -end drops due to HHS-related payments ), stable dealer balance sheets, and accelerated growth in money market fund assets accompanied by a decline in the weighted average maturity of their holdings . We exit our position for a loss of 2bp but continue to expect marginal tightening in repo spreads into the fall . We maintain our view that SOFR/FF should settle within an equilibrium range of −2bp and −4bp until debt ceiling dynamics return in late 2027. Such a move could trigger a reevaluation of the USD’s reserve status, potentially resulting in large outflow s from the US Treasury market and pushing up back-end US yields significantly : exactly what the Treasury is trying to avoid at present, in our view . By contrast, multilateral intervention s are rare and tend to occur during periods of heightened volatility that present a contagion risk to the global financial system. In the last 30 years, the US has joined forces with peers on only three occasions : during the Asian Financial Crisis, after the introduction of the EUR, and after the 2011 Japan earthquake . Historically, this coordinated action tend s to be effective. As such, the natural question is : with the US now reportedly joining forces with Japan, does this change the outlook for USDJPY? We are not yet convinced. While the risk –reward for long USDJPY is less attractive than it was before the intervention late last week, we still believe that the pair will end the year higher than current levels (see Stopping out of long USDJPY , dated 3 August). The primary reason is that the recent intervention is somewhat of a midway point between a unilateral and a multilateral intervention. In previous multilateral intervention s, participating central banks issued press s tatements on the exact intervention dates to telegraph their joint support. Policymakers in Europe may view intervention -driven EUR weakness with caution, particularly as the risk of currency depreciation could potentially complicate efforts to manage second -round inflationary effects stemming from the energy shock. Without overt ECB support , we think any Treasury intervention s are likely to be limited. FX intervention by the Treasury occurs via the funds made available through the Exchange Stabilization Fund (ESF). As of the latest disclosure (ending 30 June 2026) this is comprised of USD24.5bn USTs, USD172.2bn in Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), and USD18.8bn in foreign currencies (EUR: 1 3bn, JPY: 5.8bn). However, of the 13bn EUR the ESF holds, the more liquid holdings are those assets with a maturity of less than 3 months, which is just 1.2bn of the total . Historically, when the US Treasury intervened , the Fed joined on a 1:1 basis, sharing the burden of intervention with its own System Open Market Account (SOMA) portfolio.
